19722-a-child-s-garden-of-verses:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote A Child's Garden of Verses for young readers, first issued in 1885. This 1916 edition gathers his poems of childhood. The contents list reads like a child's day: Bed in Summer, Young Night Thought, Pirate Story. Other favorites include The Land of Counterpane and Farewell to the Farm. Stevenson treats small moments as full adventures.

A sickly child himself, Stevenson knew beds, gardens, and long indoor hours. His verses turn those limits into kingdoms. Soldiers march across a bedspread; shadows become playmates. The poems speak in a child's voice without talking down. Few children's books from the era are still read aloud. This one never left the nursery shelf.
19762-how-to-eat-a-cure-for-nerves:
Thomas Clark Hinkle, a physician, published How to Eat in 1921. Its subtitle promises a cure for nerves. Hinkle tells of a man who scorned a remedy too simple to respect. He borrows the Bible scene where servants urge a proud sufferer to try the plain cure anyway. If the prophet had demanded something great, they ask, would he not have done it?

Diet cures for nervous illness were a thriving genre then. Hinkle argues eating habits drive much nervous misery. Simple rules, faithfully kept, are his prescription. The book mixes medicine, morals, and common sense. It shows how doctors sold self-discipline as therapy. Modern readers will judge its claims for themselves.
19766-young-lucretia-and-other-stories:
Mary E. Wilkins Freeman wrote Young Lucretia and Other Stories in 1892. The title story turns on a village judging a child. One woman, the choir's soprano, sees little to pity in Lucretia's case. Most children, she says sharply, are cared for no better. Freeman lets small talk carry big moral weight. Her New England villages run on such talk.

Freeman was a master of the regional short story. Her women and children live under tight custom and tighter money. Small kindnesses and small cruelties decide their days. These stories show her quiet, exact style. Nothing loud happens; everything matters. Readers who like Chekhov's restraint will feel at home. It is American realism at village scale.
19781-sketches:
Benjamin Disraeli's Sketches collect his early short fiction and tales. One scene shows the Lady Imogene leaving Charolois by a postern gate. She is the bereaved count's only remaining child. Her page follows, bearing her book of prayers. She walks the undulating heights toward a sanctuary. The manner is romantic, youthful, and theatrical.

Disraeli wrote these pieces before fame, politics, or the premiership. He was trying voices: the tale, the sketch, the Eastern romance. Editors of the day printed such work in magazines and annuals. The Sketches let readers watch a famous style forming. His later novels keep this love of scene and costume. Here it appears young, lush, and unguarded.
19802-cobwebs-and-cables:
Hesba Stretton wrote Cobwebs and Cables as a novel of conscience and city life. It opens at eleven at night in a handsome office. Roland Sefton sits unmoving by the chimney-piece clock. He has not stirred hand or foot for a long while. He seems bound by many strong cords. The stillness signals a man trapped by his own affairs.

Stretton was famous for tales of street children and quiet sacrifice. Her novels press faith against money and reputation. An office at midnight suggests ledgers that will not balance morally. Sefton's paralysis is the story's first clue. Victorian readers trusted Stretton for earnest, unsparing plots. This opening shows her method: one still figure, much implied.
19813-ade-s-fables:
George Ade published Ade's Fables in 1912, modern fables in slang. One speaker here is a Larva with large ambitions. It wants to grow up to be a Joey, a circus clown. It aches to drive a trick mule behind the band. Little pieces of looking glass would glitter in the harness. Scared country girls peeking from wagon beds are its dream audience.

Ade rewrote Aesop for American towns and boosters. Each fable ends in a moral, often bent sideways. His slang was famous enough to define an era's humor. Politicians, farmers, and climbers all take their turns. The Larva's circus dream mocks every small-town ambition. Ade's fables remain readable because the types remain.
19825-herself-talks-with-women-concernin:
E. B. Lowry, a woman physician, wrote Herself as talks with women concerning themselves. She begins with structure before care. Readers must know something of the female generative organs first, she says. The first talk therefore teaches anatomy plainly. Lowry wrote several such guides for women and girls. Shame kept many readers ignorant of their own bodies.

Plain medical talk for women was a reform cause then. Lowry's books sold widely and were often reprinted. She treats readers as capable students, not patients to frighten. Illustrations and direct language carry her lessons. The series helped normalize women's health education. Herself is a landmark of that popular movement.
19848-woman-and-womanhood-a-search-for-p:
C. W. Saleeby published Woman and Womanhood in 1911, subtitled A Search for Principles. He opens by widening a common saying. Woman is half the human race, he grants. But present woman is also half of all generations to come. That makes her share larger than half, he argues. The book applies biology to women's social place.

Saleeby was a physician and a vocal eugenics supporter. His principles claim scientific ground for social claims. Modern readers will reject parts of that framework. The book still matters as evidence of its moment. Suffrage, motherhood, and race filled its debates. Saleeby shows how science-talk served those arguments. It is a document of Edwardian gender ideology.
19867-frank-merriwell-junior-s-golden-tr:
Burt L. Standish was Gilbert Patten's pen name for the Merriwell stories. Frank Merriwell Junior's Golden Trail sends young Frank west. Only Merry and his two chums watch from the grand stand. A practice game pits the Ophir Athletic Club eleven against a scrub team. The game was staged for Frank's exclusive benefit. From football the trail turns toward a fugitive professor.

Frank Merriwell was the dime novel's model college hero. His son inherited the name and the adventures. Sports open most Merriwell tales before mystery takes over. The Golden Trail mixes gridiron, West, and pursuit. Millions of boys followed these stories weekly. Junior's trail shows the franchise passing generations.
19892-the-silver-crown-another-book-of-f:
Laura E. Richards wrote The Silver Crown as another book of fables in 1906. One fable sends a child riding and running his best. He crosses hills and valleys, broad streams and foaming torrents. He looks eagerly at people at work or at play. The journey itself is the lesson in her hands. Richards, daughter of Julia Ward Howe, wrote beloved children's verse.

Her fables dress small morals in bright, brief tales. Kings, children, and talking things share her pages. The Silver Crown followed her earlier fable collections. She aimed at wonder first and teaching second. That order kept her books in print for decades. This volume shows her gentle, musical method.
19906-winning-a-cause-world-war-stories:
Winning a Cause, dated 1919, gathers World War stories edited by John Gilbert Thompson. Its framing notes America's slow road into the war. Her people believed war an evil to be avoided, it says. Peace at any price seemed many Americans' motto. That held even after two years of world war. The stories then show what changed those minds. Thompson wrote and edited school readers for years.

War story collections taught patriotism to the young. Short tales of soldiers and helpers carry the cause. Thompson's framing admits the nation's reluctance honestly. That honesty makes the conversion story stronger. Schools bought such volumes for postwar classrooms. The book is civic instruction in story form.
19962-piccaninnies:
Piccaninnies is a picture book of brown babies for young children. Its little ones wear decorations in their hair. They are the jolliest, tubbiest, brownest babies imaginable, the text coos. Tiny knobs on their shoulders suggest wings that never grew. The fancy is that they almost became angels or birds. Such nursery books traded in racial whimsy typical of their day. Modern readers will see the period's stereotypes plainly.

Edwardian picture books often used exotic children as decoration. Piccaninnies belongs to that uncomfortable shelf. Its verses aim at tenderness, within the limits of 1900s attitudes. Preserving it shows how empire entered the nursery. The book is evidence, charming in craft and dated in outlook. It should be read with both facts in mind.
20017-pages-for-laughing-eyes:
Pages for Laughing Eyes is a story book for young children. Jessie receives a pretty French doll from her aunt Amy in one tale. For weeks she thinks she has nothing more to wish for. Then spring comes, warm and sunny, calling her outdoors. A doll proves inconvenient to carry everywhere she goes. The story follows that small, real problem gently. Margaret Gatty's circle produced such nursery volumes.

Victorian story books for the very young prized short, bright episodes. Dolls, gardens, and siblings carry their whole drama. Jessie's doll poses the classic toy problem: love versus freedom. The laughing eyes of the title are the readers' own. Illustrations and large print served new readers well. It is a sweet fossil of the nursery shelf.
20034-scottish-ghost-stories:
Scottish ghost stories fill these pages, told in the first person by a man drawn back to Perthshire. He answers an ad in a ladies' weekly paper. It offers a snug home at fair terms in an older Highland lady's house. The house stands at Pitlochry, a town he knew as a boy.

From that calm start, the tales turn to strange sights and uneasy nights. Scotland's hills, old houses, and oral tales give the scares their shape. Readers who like slow, place-based ghost tales will find that mood here. Dread builds from setting more than from shock.
20044-riders-of-the-silences:
John Frederick published Riders of the Silences in 1920, a western novel with a priest at its heart. Father Anthony holds the warmth of the short northern summer, the book says. His kind face draws people as hands reach toward a fire. Chapter titles promise a small voice, a night voice, and a man's death.

The tale moves through cross, storm, and hard choices on a cold frontier. Good nature meets violence in a land of silences. Readers get a western with a strong moral core. Faith, not just gunplay, drives much of the action here.
20076-rimrock-jones:
Rimrock Jones is a western novel set in a rough mining town of the American West. Ore cars bang along the sidings toward bins and chutes. A switch engine snorts and clangs while the town stays still. That mix of noise and calm opens the tale in sharp strokes.

Western tales of this kind turn on claims, cash, and hard men. Rimrock, whose name evokes desert rock rims, stands at the centre. Readers get dust, rail, and ore as the stage for greed and grit. The town's wealth lies in the ground, and so do its fights.
20112-lill-s-travels-in-santa-claus-land:
Ellis Towne, Sophie May, and Ella Farman wrote Lill's Travels in Santa Claus Land, plus other stories. Lill walks far and comes to a high wall built into the sky. At first she thinks she has found the ends of the earth. It might even be the great wall of China, she thinks.

Then she finds a large gate with gold words above it. The words, big enough for a baby to read, name Santa Claus Land. From there, a child's dream trip through Christmas magic begins. The tales mix wonder, morals, and holiday cheer for young readers.
20124-be-arn-and-the-pyrenees:
Louisa Stuart Costello wrote Béarn and the Pyrenees, a legendary tour to the land of Henri Quatre. Costello traveled in France and wrote of its towns, tales, and past. Each step opened new stores of interest, she tells her readers. Encouraged by praise, she set out again by a fresh route.

Her road ran through Champagne and Burgundy to Rheims and Bourges. Vine-covered plains, old cathedrals, and storied palaces fill the pages. Legends cling to the Pyrenees and to Henri, the beloved king. Readers get travel writing rich in history, myth, and bright local detail.
20127-here-are-ladies:
Here Are Ladies is a book of tales and sketches about women and love. One man states a harsh rule for all he claims as his. If a thing lives, he demands its duty to the last breath. If it is dead, he will allow no claim on it at all.

Such stark words hint at pride, control, and tangled hearts within. Short pieces let the writer try many voices and fates in turn. Love in these pages is rarely calm or simple for long. Readers get a set of keen, varied studies of women and the men around them.
20139-old-fogy-his-musical-opinions-and-:
James Huneker wrote Old Fogy, a book of musical opinions and grotesques, issued in 1913. Huneker was a sharp, witty critic of music and books in New York. He asks if Mozart is not still young, gay, and full of mischief. Beethoven, he says, stays virile, earnest, and noble in his scores.

Bach seems oldest of the three, yet his preludes belie his years. The Well-Tempered Clavichord grows younger with time, Huneker claims. His essays mix deep love of music with jokes and bold takes. Readers get criticism with flair, bite, and real knowledge behind it.
20183-john-quincy-adams-american-statesm:
John Quincy Adams fills this life in the American Statesmen series, from 1882. Adams became minister at The Hague in 1794, early in his career. From then till his death in February 1848, he stayed in public life. The book still fits that long career in some three hundred pages.

Its aim, the preface says, is to draw a picture of the man. Adams served as diplomat, senator, secretary of state, president, and congressman. Few Americans matched that span of service across so many posts. Readers get a compact, admiring life of a stern, gifted statesman.
20196-victorian-worthies:
G. H. Blore wrote Victorian Worthies, sixteen biographies of notable Victorians. Blore muses that each age has a character and face of its own. The sixteenth century speaks of change and adventure in every form. Ships, statecraft, discovery, and masterful rulers fill that age's tale.

Against such color, the Victorian age can seem plain at first glance. Blore's sixteen lives argue that its worthies hold their own in worth. Statesmen, writers, and reformers pass in clear, brief portraits. Readers get a handy gallery of the men who shaped Victorian Britain.
20231-earth-s-enigmas-a-volume-of-storie:
Earth's Enigmas, from 1895, is a volume of stories of wild life and strange nature. A great panther slips from a shadowy hollow behind a white rock. In daylight his coat would show a warm, tawny hue. In moonlight he wears a spectral gray as he lifts his head.

He greets a growing flame with a shrill, eerie cry. Such tales blend keen nature watching with mystery and dread. The writer knew Canadian woods and beasts from long study afield. Readers get outdoor stories where nature holds secrets man cannot tame.
20237-art-in-england-notes-and-studies:
Dutton Cook wrote Art in England, notes and studies on English painting and taste. Charles the First, Cook argues, first prized art for its own sake. Earlier rulers used art mainly to add splendor to the throne. Walpole quipped that Elizabeth was avaricious with pomp, James lavish with meanness.

To neither earlier ruler did a painter's standing matter at all. Cook traces how artists slowly won respect and support in England. His studies mix lives, schools, and sharp critical judgments. Readers get a clear survey of English art as Victorians understood it.
20286-funny-alphabet-uncle-franks-series:
Funny Alphabet, in Uncle Frank's series, is a picture alphabet book for young children. Such books pair each letter with a comic verse and a bright picture. Children learn their letters while laughing at odd beasts and men. Uncle Frank's series was a known line of cheap, cheerful children's books.

Alphabet books were often a child's first book of their own. Short rhymes make each letter stick in a young mind with ease. The fun comes first, and the lesson rides in on its back. Young readers of the era got letters, pictures, and giggles in one slim volume.
20308-white-ashes:
Kennedy-Noble published White Ashes in 1912, a novel of ruin and slow reckoning. One man stares into the eyes of utter, absolute ruin at last. Yet that day is premature when the tale first opens wide. Much water must flow under many bridges before it arrives.

The story deals with some of that flowing water, step by step. White ashes suggest burned-out hopes, spent fires, and what remains after. Business, love, and pride often drive such Edwardian tales of fall. Readers get a grave novel of consequence built at a measured pace.
20315-the-grasshopper-stories:
Elizabeth Davis Leavitt published The Grasshopper Stories in 1912, tales for young children. A little tin soldier seems to urge Billy to march with him. A toy horse and wagon stand ready to start a journey. A teddy bear, head on one side, seems to invite a romp.

Toys that speak in a child's mind fill these warm, small tales. Billy's playroom world turns each object into a friend with a voice. Leavitt writes in short, clear scenes a young child can follow. Readers get gentle stories where play itself becomes the adventure.
20329-negritos-of-zambales:
Negritos of Zambales is an ethnological study of a people in the Philippines. Maps show the spread of Negritos across the Philippine Islands. Photos show Negrito men and women of Bataan and Zambales. One view compares the heights of American, mixed, and pure Negrito figures.

American-era scholars recorded language, custom, and daily life in such reports. Zambales, on Luzon's west coast, held many small, forest-dwelling communities. The study reflects both real field data and the biases of its time. Readers get a dated but detailed record of a people and place.
20345-old-man-savarin-and-other-stories:
Old Man Savarin and Other Stories holds Canadian tales of river and woods life. A fisherman declares he has had enough fishing for his age. He offers six or seven doré, a fine freshwater fish, as a gift. In return, he asks just one quarter dollar in exchange.

Such talk, in French-Canadian dialect, gives the tales their warm flavor. Savarin is an old riverman whose yarns anchor the title story. Gilbert Parker wrote of Canadian life with love for its two tongues. Readers get northern tales of fish, faith, and sly rural bargaining.
20351-jackanapes:
Jackanapes is a beloved children's tale set on a village Goose Green. Two donkeys and the geese live on the Green itself there. All other residents of standing live in houses round it. The houses have no names, and every address is just The Green.

Yet the postman and local people know where each family lives. Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote this tale of a brave, merry boy. Jackanapes rides, laughs, and at last gives his life for a friend. Generations have wept and smiled over this short, perfect children's classic.
20353-the-best-nonsense-verses:
The Best Nonsense Verses, from 1901, gathers comic rhymes by masters of nonsense. One famous verse has a youth quiz his aged, aged man. Your jaws are too weak for anything tougher than suet, he says. Yet you finished the goose, with bones and beak, the youth protests.

Pray, how did you manage to do it, he asks in wonder. That poem is Edward Lear's or Lewis Carroll's kind of joyful absurdity. Nonsense verse delights by sound, logic twisted, and pure surprise. Readers get a classic anthology of the form at its playful best.
20365-the-young-mountaineers-short-stori:
Published in 1897, The Young Mountaineers gathers short stories set in the high mountain country of the American South. The author's name is not given in this edition. Cabins stand on ravine slopes, and steep crags and cliffs shape the world the characters live in.

The tales follow mountain folk at home and on the trails, told with a strong feel for local speech and custom. One scene shows a man smoking his pipe outside a cabin, gazing at a cliff face known as Old Daddy's Window. Readers get a close picture of the hard, quiet daily life of remote mountain settlements.
20366-wonderwings-and-other-fairy-storie:
Edith Howes wrote these fairy stories for young readers, and the title tale gives the book its name. In it, a small fairy named Poppypink meets a visitor called Wonderwings. The visitor is taller and more beautiful than any other fairy there, and her wings explain her name at once.

Howes fills her tales with gentle magic, small adventures, and the everyday doings of tiny fairy folk. The stories are told in simple, warm language that suits reading aloud. They show the kind of soft, kind fairy tale that was popular with children in the early years of the last century.
20370-rhymes-of-the-east-and-re-collecte:
Rhymes of the East and Re-collected Verses brings together light verse, much of it first printed in magazines. The poems play with news, travel, and the odd habits of British life abroad. The tone is comic and dry rather than grand.

One poem mocks the way alarming news travels from ear to ear. Knowledge, it says, pours out her latest store, and the source, once known, would freeze the heart. The verses suit readers who like short, witty poems that poke fun at gossip, empire, and everyday pride. Most are short enough to finish in a minute, and sharp enough to remember all day.
20380-ten-tales:
Ten Tales, published in 1890, is a set of ten short stories that range widely in mood. The set runs from the tragic adventure of An Accident to the paired portraits of the Two Clowns. That second tale cuts with sarcasm, the book's guide notes, but it is not bitter.

Another story, The Captain's Vices, is compared with George Eliot's Silas Marner for its grip. The tales move between sea life, crime, character study, and sharp social comedy. Together they show the short story form at a time when magazine fiction was at its height.
20403-a-fearful-responsibility-and-other:
A Fearful Responsibility and Other Stories, published in 1881, gathers tales of American and European life. In one story, a man named Elmore is pressed to go on with his history of Venice. His friend urges him to travel to Venice and gather his materials on the spot.

War news runs under the talk. Seward puts the conflict at sixty days, but the speaker gives the rebels six months to lay down their arms. Such details fix the stories in the Civil War years and just after. The tales turn on duty, love, and the weight of promises.
20420-real-ghost-stories:
William T. Stead, the famous journalist, collected and edited Real Ghost Stories from accounts sent to him and gathered from print. He weighed the title with care before keeping it. The word ghost, he notes, had lost its true meaning for many modern readers.

Most people tie ghosts to haunted houses and weird sights that fill them with dread. Stead wanted the older, wider sense of the word: spirits and apparitions of many kinds. The reports in the book range across homes, ships, and lonely roads, and they show how strongly Victorians hunted for proof of the unseen.
20425-the-peace-egg-and-other-tales:
The Peace Egg and Other Tales gathers stories and a traditional Christmas play for young readers. The Peace Egg is an old mummers' play, performed here by children. Most of the actors were too young to learn long parts.

That hardly hurt the show. There was little of the tedious dialogue, the teller says, and plenty of dress and ribbons instead. The fighters dueled with wooden swords to great effect. The other tales in the book share that warm, home-made feel, mixing old custom with gentle fun for the nursery and the schoolroom.
20437-the-frog-prince-and-other-stories:
Walter Crane, one of the great illustrators of children's books, presents The Frog Prince and Other Stories. The title tale retells the old fairy tale of the princess and the frog. Its dialogue follows the classic bargain closely.

The frog asks for no dresses, jewels, or golden crowns. He asks to be her companion and playfellow, to sit at her table and eat from her little golden plate. He wants to drink from her cup and sleep in her little bed. Crane's pictures and the plain retelling made such tales nursery standards.
20438-moriah-s-mourning-and-other-half-h:
Ruth McEnery Stuart published Moriah's Mourning and Other Half-Hour Sketches in 1898. The sketches draw on life in the plantation country of the South. She writes in local dialect, with humor and a sharp ear for talk.

The title sketch turns on the rules for wearing mourning dress. In plantation communities, Stuart notes, those rules are by no means strict. A widow who wears out her colored clothes during working hours, for economy or ease, is not called to account for it. The book catches the customs and speech of its region with fond precision.
20486-tiverton-tales:
Alice Brown set her Tiverton Tales in a New England village she knew well. The tales watch farm and village folk at their daily work. Hens, yards, and gardens matter as much as sermons and town meetings.

One narrator admits that careless householders feed the hens in the yard. Then they shoo the birds away when the hens take dust baths under the syringa bush. The hens leave unsightly hollows in the flower beds. Such small scenes, told with dry humor and local speech, build a full portrait of village life as Brown's readers remembered it.
20491-kafir-stories-seven-short-stories:
Kafir Stories collects seven short stories of life in South Africa, written when the region's peoples were being drawn into a new order. The tales look at African life through the eyes of a settler writer of the time. An old poem stands at the head of the book.

The verse tells how fate leads through a garden of three trees: Knowledge, Death, and Life. On one tree wholesome fruit grows, and on another, fair fruit with poison mixed in. Sometimes apples prove deadly, it warns, while poisoned fruits may nourish. The stories that follow keep that note of moral uncertainty.
20493-stories-and-sketches: Stories and Sketches gathers tales for young readers, among them one of a boy named Terry. Other boys taunted Terry with a nickname that mocked his odd looks. They soon learned to keep a safe distance before using that name. Terry's anger at the taunt was more than they cared to face twice. The sketches mix schoolboy justice with moral turns.
20497-bucholz-and-the-detectives:
Bucholz and the Detectives narrates a case from the files of a great American detective agency. The narrator presents it as a true story of detective experience. He says it is in many respects both peculiar and interesting.

The case, he argues, proves one of the cardinal principles of his detective system. The agency's method rested on patience, disguise, and never dropping a trail. In these memoirs, criminals are tracked across cities and countries until the evidence closes in. Readers of the time devoured such books as fact, and they shaped the popular image of the private detective.
20510-ade-s-fables:
George Ade's Fables, published in 1912, retells Aesop for modern America. Ade wrote in slangy, capital-lettered prose that made him famous. Each fable ends with a moral twisted for the age of money and hustle.

One fable opens with Ambition in person. Ambition came, with Sterling Silver Breast-Plate and Flaming Sword, and sat beside a Tad aged five. The wee hopeful lived in a frame house with box pillars in front and hollyhocks leading down toward the pike. Ade's mix of fairy-tale dress and street talk lets him mock climbers, lovers, and boosters with a grin.
20541-the-rocky-island-and-other-similit:
The Rocky Island and Other Similitudes teaches spiritual lessons through pictured scenes, in the manner of a parable. A similitude works like a small allegory: an island, a garden, or a road stands for the life of the soul. Such books were written for children and for family reading.

The Rocky Island first looks sad and dreary, covered with broken pieces on all sides. The narrator thought no one could dwell in it. Looking closer, he saw its shores covered with children at play, on a soft white sand. The turn from dread to joy carries the lesson of the piece.
20552-roumanian-fairy-tales:
Roumanian Fairy Tales collects the wonder tales of Romanian peasants, gathered from village tellers and printed for English readers. The tales open in the classic way. At the edge of a village, the first story begins, where the peasants' oxen break through the hedges.

There the neighbors' hogs wallow in the ground under the fences, and there once stood a house. In the house lived a man, and the man had a wife, but the wife grieved. From such plain starts the tales run to enchanted princes, dragons, and clever youngest sons, in the rich tradition of Romanian folklore.
20590-letters-lettering-a-treatise-with-:
Letters and Lettering, published in 1921, is a treatise on the design of letters, with two hundred examples. It was written for architects, sign painters, and draftsmen who had to draw fine lettering by hand. Frank Chouteau Brown based the lessons on classic forms.

The first point to observe, he writes, is the Roman capital's characteristic squareness. The letter used today varies somewhat in proportion from its classic model. But its skeleton is still based on the square and the circle of the old Roman form. The book's plates let students copy good alphabets stroke by stroke.
20642-the-assemble-of-goddes:
The Assemble of Goddes is a Middle English dream poem, printed here in a scholarly edition. In the poem, the gods gather in assembly, and the dreamer watches their debate. The text comes down in old spelling, with the thorn and yogh letters of medieval writing.

The edition explains its marks for the reader. A little e written over the Middle English thorn stands for the word the. A little t over the thorn means that, and a little u means thou. A small t over a w stands for with. Such keys let modern readers enter a poem few could otherwise read.
20655-the-emma-gees:
Herbert W. McBride's The Emma Gees, published in 1918, is a First World War memoir of the machine gunners. Emma Gee was the soldiers' phonetic name for M.G., machine gun. McBride served with Canadian troops and wrote the war's classic account of snipers and machine-gun crews.

He explains the signalers' spelling alphabet along the way. Letters with similar sounds, such as S and F, or M and N, caused many mistakes in messages. So the signaler's ingenuity invented distinct names for the letters most alike. McBride mixes such craft detail with grim, exact battle writing.
20707-the-black-star-passes:
John W. Campbell's The Black Star Passes, published in book form in 1953, collects his early stories of the space engineers Arcot, Morey, and Wade. Campbell wrote them nearly a quarter of a century before, for the old Amazing Stories magazine. His introduction defends that magazine's spirit.

The essence of any magazine, Campbell writes, is not its name but its philosophy and purpose. That old Amazing Stories is long since gone, he admits. Its purpose — science told as adventure — lives in these tales of a black star's passing and the machines men build to meet it. Campbell later reshaped the field as an editor.
20710-pluck-on-the-long-trail-or-boy-sco:
Edwin L. Sabin's Pluck on the Long Trail, published in 1912, sends a troop of Boy Scouts into the Rockies. Its subtitle names them Boy Scouts in the Rockies. The boys track, camp, and climb through a long mountain journey, with pluck as their chief supply.

Scouts in America, Sabin writes, have a high honor to maintain. The American scout has always been the best in the world: keen, quick, cautious, and brave. He teaches himself, and he is willing to be taught by others. Such passages made the book a recruiting sermon for the young scouting movement, wrapped in a mountain adventure.
20718-the-damsel-and-the-sage-a-woman-s-:
The Damsel and the Sage: A Woman's Whimsies, published in 1903, stages dialogues between a young woman and an old philosopher. She questions him on love, men, and life, and he answers in fables and paradoxes. The whimsies of the subtitle are pointed little tales slipped into the talk.

One fable tells of a man who found a spare ear on his path. A man of greater shrewdness came along and said a third ear would not come amiss. He picked it up and heard with three ears instead of two, and so became knowing and clever. The dialogues sparkle with such sly turns.
20748-favorite-fairy-tales:
Snow-White grows fairer each year in Favorite Fairy Tales, until at age seven she outshines the Queen. The Queen turns to her mirror for the truth she fears. That mirror sets one of the world's best-known tales in motion.

Alongside Snow-White, this set holds other dear tales for young readers. Wicked queens, kind children, magic helpers, and just ends follow the classic pattern. The plain retelling suits reading aloud at home or school. Such books kept the old European tales alive for each new crop of children, in words simple enough for the youngest listener to follow.
20774-the-shanty-book-part-i-sailor-shan:
Sailors' work songs fill The Shanty Book, Part One, from 1921. The foreword praises Captain Whall's book, which gave tunes without full backing. This new set aims wider, to gather a full, fair stock of shanties in one place.

Shanties timed the heave and haul of shipboard work at sea. Each song here pairs words with music for singers to use. Richard Runciman Terry, a church musician, took sea songs with real care. His book helped carry shanties from tall ships to concert rooms and folk clubs, where they still ring out today.
20831-short-stories-of-various-types:
High school pupils stand at the front of Short Stories of Various Types, from 1920. The editor chose tales of varied style and lands for first-year high school use. Plots of many types aim at the interests of young readers just waking to books.

Classroom sets like this one shaped the taste of a whole school generation. Each tale shows a distinct plot kind, from surprise ends to character sketches. Notes and choice were meant to teach what makes a story work. The book is a neat fossil of how English was taught in American schools a century ago.
20853-northland-heroes:
Ingeborg, a king's daughter, and Frithiof, a viking's son, grow up in one garden. Florence Holbrook opens Northland Heroes in the home of Hilding, their foster father. Kings Bele and Thorsten, fast friends, entrust their children to his care.

Norse sagas of love, sea roving, and honour fill Holbrook's retelling for the young. Frithiof's deeds and his love for Ingeborg drive the central tale. Holbrook, a Chicago school leader, shaped classic tales for classroom use. Her clear prose lets young readers meet the North's stark, brave world without the maze of the old saga tongue.
20870-the-motor-girls-through-new-englan:
Cora Kimball pauses to fix her car, the Whirlwind, with a wrench from the tool box. Margaret Penrose's Motor Girls Through New England, from 1911, keeps its heroines at the wheel. Mail waits in a box while the girls hold back from a house till friends come.

Motoring tours, Gypsy camps, and roadside scrapes fill this girls' series tale. The Motor Girls drove their own cars when few women did. Penrose gives them grit, skill, and good cheer on New England roads. The book captures the thrill of early motoring, when a tour by car still felt like bold adventure.
20889-facts-about-champagne-and-other-sp:
No pains or cost were spared, says the preface, to make Facts About Champagne full and exact. Fine engravings aid the text at each turn, the editor adds with pride. Henry Vizetelly, a wine writer of note, gathered the facts from the ground up.

Champagne country, cellars, makers, and rival sparkling wines fill his brisk survey. Vizetelly knew the trade from years of travel and trade in wine. He sorts true champagne from mere fizz with a dealer's sharp eye. The book froze the wine world of the 1870s in print, when champagne ruled fine tables on both sides of the sea.
20898-the-galaxy-primes:
A coin flip picks Jim for Lola in The Galaxy Primes, with a sneer at the system's best. James James James the Ninth bears his grand name into deep peril. E. E. Smith sets supermen and superwomen loose among the stars here.

Primes, the peak of human breed and skill, must crew a ship flung far from home. Smith piles vast space, strange worlds, and mind powers at pulp speed. The tale first ran in magazines before its book form. Readers who love Smith's Lensman scale will find the same bold hand, with a new crew and a fresh, wild reach of space.
20916-the-arabian-nights-their-best-know:
A joyful dawn breeze fills the sail of youth in the verse that fronts The Arabian Nights. Down the Tigris, past Baghdad's gold shrines, the singer was borne in Haroun Alraschid's prime. Kate Douglas Wiggin's 1909 set of best-known tales opens in that glow.

Sinbad, Aladdin, Ali Baba, and Scheherazade herself star in these retellings. Wiggin and Nora Smith chose and smoothed tales for young readers at home. Magic lamps, caves of gems, and bold voyages fill the pages. This set served as many children's first door into the Nights, kept rich in wonder and pruned for family reading.
20962-sandman-s-goodnight-stories:
Dicky Duck, too sure of his own wit, swims straight toward Mr. Fox in Sandman's Goodnight Stories. Abbie Phillips Walker's 1921 tales tuck such small perils into bedtime form. The fox hides in the woods by the pond, keen and still.

Walker wrote gentle animal tales to read aloud as children drift to sleep. Ducks, rabbits, and other small beasts learn care, kindness, and sense. Each tale stays short, warm, and safe in its close. The book shows the bedtime story trade at its sweetest, made by a teller who knew just how much scare a small listener can bear.
20983-robert-hardy-s-seven-days-a-dream-:
The dullest sermon Robert Hardy ever heard starts his seven days of change. Charles Sheldon puts Hardy's scorn for old Jones and his soul-saving talk up front. A dream then tests what a week of true change might look like.

Sheldon, author of In His Steps, wrote tales that press faith into daily acts. Hardy, a young lawyer, dreams a week lived on higher terms. Work, money, and home all shift under that dream's stern light. The book shows Sheldon's creed in story form: ask what Christ would do, then do it, for one week or for life.
21004-the-singing-mouse-stories:
A worn coat, a broken rifle stock, and a frayed fishing rod open The Singing Mouse Stories. Emerson Hough speaks as an old hand whose gear bears a life's marks. That rueful, warm voice frames his tales of field and camp from 1910.

Hough, who wrote The Covered Wagon, here gathers slight, charmed nature tales. Mice that sing, old guns, and mountain camps fill his pages with lore. He writes as a sportsman who loves the wild more than the bag. These stories show his gentler side, far from epic treks, in small wonders noted by firelight.
21008-the-boy-with-the-u-s-fisheries:
A cry from the masthead barrel sends Colin Dare leaping up by a broken whale gun. The Boy with the U.S. Fisheries promises him a boat if a whale is sighted. Francis Rolt-Wheeler fills his tale with ships, fish, and federal service.

Rolt-Wheeler's U.S. Service set put boys inside real government work of all kinds. Fisheries patrols, hatcheries, and sea hunts fill this volume's brisk plot. Facts ride on adventure's back in his trusted formula for boys. Readers learn how America guarded its fish wealth while cheering a lad's rise through pluck and work.
21012-the-loyalists-of-america-and-their:
Misjudged and maligned, the Loyalists get a defence built on their own records here. Egerton Ryerson refuses mere claim against claim in The Loyalists of America and Their Times. Their own words, he vows, shall correct the unjust tale told of them.

Loyalists who kept faith with Britain lost homes in the American Revolution. Ryerson, a Canadian leader, traces their trials, exile, and new lives in Canada. Documents bulk large, by design, in his two-volume history. The book stands as a founding brief for the Loyalist claim on Canada's past and pride.
21014-wonder-box-tales:
Each forest once held a wood king who taxed woodmen in kindling blocks, Jean Ingelow recounts. Wonder-Box Tales, from 1902, opens on that quaint report of old country lore. Such tales were told to her great-great-grandmother's age, she notes with a smile.

Ingelow, a beloved Victorian teller, gathers fairy tales of wonder and gentle moral weight. Kings of the wood, spells, and small heroes fill her warm pages. Her tales favour kindness and wonder over fright and gore. This late set shows her art undimmed, a grandmotherly voice still sure of its young hearers' hearts.
21039-boycotted-and-other-stories:
Browne's loss drains Draven's of all spirit in Boycotted, Talbot Baines Reed's lead tale. Football lacks its place-kick, Saturday nights their singer, reciter, and orator in one. Study suppers lose their point when there is no Browne to invite.

Short school tales fill this set, each built on Reed's sure knowledge of boys. Boycott, feuds, games, and house pride drive the plots in brisk turns. Reed gathers here the kind of pieces that filled The Boy's Own Paper's pages. Together they show his range in miniature, humour and pathos packed into tales that never outstay their welcome.
21040-brazilian-tales:
Brazilian Portuguese strays further from its parent tongue than American English does, this intro argues. The editor's notes weigh language as a key to Brazil's separate soul. Brazilian Tales, from 1921, brings that land's stories to English readers.

Machado de Assis and other masters of Brazilian prose star in these versions. Isaac Goldberg chose and turned tales of love, irony, and city life. Brazil's letters were then near unknown in English, a gap this book fills. Readers meet a literature of rare polish and bite, still too little read outside its own rich tongue.
21073-a-pirate-of-the-caribbees:
Young officer Courtenay wakes to eight bells in the midshipmen's berth of the frigate Althea in Harry Collingwood's Caribbean tale. His task through the story is to bring a wicked pirate named Morillo to justice. The hunt plays out across the Caribbees in mid-Atlantic and island waters.

Shipwrecks, captures, hurricanes, and founderings come at the usual Collingwood pace, yet the tale stays plausible in its sea work. Courtenay serves, fights, and pursues while the pirate stays a step ahead. For readers of boys' naval fiction, it offers a clear hero, a clear villain, and a chase that fills a whole cruise.
21092-on-the-trail-of-the-space-pirates:
Carey Rockwell's Tom Corbett, Space Cadet adventure appeared in 1953, with Willy Ley as technical adviser. It opens at the New Chicago Monorail Terminal, where Tom and his unit mates Astro and Roger wait among crowds for the Atom City express. Their first stop is Space Academy.

The cadets belong to a unit of the Solar Guard, the space force of their future world. Pirates threaten shipping among the planets, and the boys are drawn onto their trail. Rocket ships, air locks, and space stations fill the action. The series was tied to the popular Tom Corbett television and radio shows of the time.
21108-fritz-and-eric-the-brother-crusoes:
Brothers Fritz and Eric take very different roads in John Conroy Hutcheson's tale. Fritz fights in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71, is badly wounded, and falls in love with the young woman who nurses him. Eric goes to sea in a rotten old ship that sinks in southern waters, and he is presumed dead.

Fritz sails for America and, chatting with a whaling captain in a bar, meets Eric alive after a unlikely rescue. The brothers persuade the whaler to land them on remote Inaccessible Island in the South Atlantic. They plan a year of sealing to make their fortunes, though fortune arrives another way.
21130-book-of-wise-sayings-selected-larg:
W. A. Clouston, a scholar of popular tales and Persian literature, collected these wise sayings in London in 1893. He drew largely on Eastern sources, as the title promises. His preface answers cynics who ask what good proverbs do, since people repeat them only after someone has gone wrong.

Clouston argues that sayings learned young return with tenfold force in middle age, often with regret that they were not followed. Short, dart-like sentences are his ideal, backed by quotes from Bacon and Milton on the title pages. The little book gathers maxims of prudence from many lands into one pocket volume.
21202-fighting-the-whales:
R. M. Ballantyne opens this whaling tale in wonder that men can kill a whale at all. It is a fish over sixty feet long, with the bulk of three hundred fat oxen. The chapters then take readers aboard a whaler for the real work. The first battle with a whale comes early.

Cutting in the blubber and trying out the oil, the greasy core of the trade, get a chapter of their own. Storms, a man overboard and rescued, fighting bulls, and a gam, a visit between ships, fill the voyage. Published by Blackie in 1915 from Ballantyne's older tale, it teaches whaling while it thrills.
21222-the-armourer-s-prentices:
Charlotte M. Yonge set this historical novel in the early years of Henry VIII, when England's religious world was starting to simmer. Two orphan brothers from Hampshire travel to London seeking relatives. On the road they rescue a leading City figure attacked by highwaymen, and so join his household.

In London the boys are apprenticed among the armourers while great changes gather around them. Dean Colet, Thomas More, and other figures of the pre-Reformation years cross their path. Questions of the King's marriages trouble the court above their workshop. Yonge, a careful student of history, mixes craft, family duty, and faith in a lively Tudor tale.
21226-christie-redfern-s-troubles:
Margaret Robertson's novel follows the Redfern family after the mother's death, when they emigrate to Canada. There they find a strong Scottish world of kirk and preacher, with many services in Gaelic, the language many settlers had spoken from birth. The family settles on a small farm.

Christie Redfern stands at the centre, and much of the action happens inside the young girls' minds rather than in big events. Neighbouring families like the Nesbitts share their standing. Robertson's books lean religious, and this one is no exception. Slow, peaceful, and observant, it follows Christie through troubles of conscience, family duty, and growing up far from Scotland.
21247-browning-s-heroines:
Ethel Colburn Mayne studies the women of Robert Browning's poems in this 1913 Chatto and Windus volume, with a frontispiece of Pippa. She sorts the heroines into girlhood, the great lady, the lover, and the wife. Pippa Passes takes four chapters, from dawn to the ending of the day.

Other chapters treat Mildred Tresham, Balaustion, and Pompilia from The Ring and the Book. My Last Duchess stands for the great lady section. James Lee's Wife and A Woman's Last Word close the wife group. Mayne reads Browning's dramatic monologues as portraits of women, asking what each reveals and hides.
21278-the-old-castle-and-other-stories:
Thomas Nelson and Sons published this children's story collection in London in 1881. It contains The Old Castle, George and Alick, The Sixpenny Calico, and A Westmoreland Story. The title tale opens on Flaxy's birthday in November, with children cosy around a parlour fire while the wind shakes the dying leaves outside.

Games, dissected maps, puzzles, and a grand romp at fox and geese fill the evening before story telling begins. One boy offers a true story about himself that does him little credit. The four tales share the Nelson house style: home scenes, honest children, and lessons carried lightly inside the fun.
21286-mother-west-wind-how-stories:
Thornton W. Burgess answers children's how-and-why questions about animals in this 1916 volume of Mother West Wind stories, illustrated by Harrison Cady. Peter Rabbit watches a black speck sail across the sky as the first tale explains how Old King Eagle won his white head. Twelve chapters follow the same pattern.

Readers learn how Old Mr. Mink taught himself to swim, how Old Mr. Toad learned to sing, and how Johnny Chuck came to sleep all winter. Burgess dedicated the book to wildlife conservation and to children's love of the Green Forest. His stories teach real animal habits inside folk-tale explanations, a method he used for decades.
21308-first-in-the-field-a-story-of-new-:
Nic Braydon is left at ten in an English boarding school while his family builds a new life in New South Wales. His father, a London doctor who worked himself ill, has turned to outdoor life on a sheep and cattle station called The Bluff. At fifteen Nic is collected and sails on the East Indiaman Northumbrian to Sydney.

George Manville Fenn peoples the station with old Samson, full of wisdom, and farm servant Brookes. Mayne, called Leather, is a well-behaved convict trusted to work the farm. A hostile neighbour at The Wattles stirs the trouble. Nic learns station life, and his place in it, the hard way.
21340-the-little-gold-miners-of-the-sier:
Joaquin Miller leads this Boston story collection of 1886 with its title tale of little gold miners in California's Sierras. Around it stand eleven more stories by other hands, most of them about children. Marion Harland contributes A Modern Hero, and Mary Catherine Lee two tales of Benny and his wigwam.

Schoolboys kill a bear in one tale, and Pete gets a printing press in another. A button boy and a doughnut bait carry other chapters, by writers including Kate Gannett Wells and James Otis. The mix shows what American Sunday school and family publishers offered young readers: western adventure, school life, and small moral victories in short, illustrated pieces.
21386-james-braithwaite-the-supercargo-t:
James Braithwaite goes to sea as a supercargo in W. H. G. Kingston's novel of adventure ashore and afloat. A supercargo is the ship's clerk for trade goods. He must know where each item of cargo lies, so it can be landed in the right order at each port.

The tale opens in wild weather at the mouth of Portsmouth Harbour, with craft of all sizes dashing about. Braithwaite's work takes him through storms, strange ports, and tight scrapes on land and sea. Kingston wrote the book late in his life, while gravely ill. Many readers rank it among his best and most skilled sea stories.
21394-priscilla-s-spies:
Frank Mannix ends the summer term as a school hero in George A. Birmingham's Priscilla's Spies, published in 1912. His fine catch and sixty not out win the cock house match for Edmonstone House. A feast and a speech from his house master crown the day.

School glory is only the start of this light, witty tale. Birmingham, an Irish cleric who wrote comic novels, sets boyish pride loose among grown-up schemes. The title hints at quiet watching and secret errands to come. Readers get crisp talk, gentle mockery of proud folk, and a plot that keeps its secrets well past the cricket field.
21407-figures-of-several-centuries:
Arthur Symons profiles great writers across many ages in Figures of Several Centuries, first published in 1916. The book opens with Saint Augustine, whose Confessions Symons calls the first life story told to God. From there it ranges through poets, saints, and novelists of many lands.

Readers meet Charles Lamb, Villon, Casanova, and John Donne in the early essays. Later pieces treat Emily Brontë, Poe, Flaubert, Swinburne, and Rossetti. Symons also writes on Ibsen, Baudelaire, Pater, and the Goncourts. Each piece is a sharp, short study of a mind and its work, written with a critic's love.
21414-culinary-herbs-their-cultivation-h:
M. G. Kains, an editor of the American Agriculturist, wrote Culinary Herbs in 1912. The book treats the growing, picking, curing, and use of kitchen herbs. It opens by recalling the plain, rich tastes of home cooking in days past.

Kains defines what counts as a kitchen herb, then takes each plant in turn. He tells how to raise fennel, balm, parsley, basil, and thyme in a home plot. He also tells how to dry and store them for the cook. Gardeners who cook, and cooks who garden, will both find plain, sound help here.
21427-comic-history-of-the-united-states:
Bill Nye retells the story of his country for laughs in his Comic History of the United States, copyrighted in 1894. F. Opper's drawings add jokes of their own to the text. The book starts, of course, with the discovery of America.

Chapters move through the colonies, Plymouth, the Charter Oak, and Dutch New York. Nye gives Washington, Franklin, and the Revolution his dry, mock-grave touch. Bull Run and the Civil War get the same treatment near the end. The humour is loose and tall-tale in style, yet the march of events stays true enough to follow with ease.
21428-goody-two-shoes:
Margery Meanwell, the girl called Goody Two-Shoes, starts life rich and ends it poor, in the 1888 picture-book version. Her father, Farmer Meanwell, lost his crops, his sheep, and at last his farm. Cruel lenders like Sir Thomas Gripe and Farmer Graspall pressed him hard.

Margery and her brother Tommy are left with almost nothing to eat or wear. Tommy has two shoes, but Margery goes barefoot, and they sleep in barns. The famed tale shows her rising by good sense, kindness, and learning. Generations of children met their first moral tale in some form of her story.
21455-dick-cheveley-his-adventures-and-m:
Dick Cheveley, a vicar's teenage son, longs for the sea in W. H. G. Kingston's Dick Cheveley. His family, above all his Aunt Deb, oppose the plan. A midshipman's place would need fifty pounds a year, and the money is not there.

Dick falls in with Mark, a boy in trouble for poaching, and betrays local smugglers. They seize him and nearly kill him for it. Later he slips aboard a ship, falls through a hatch, and wakes trapped in the hold at sea. A cruel captain, weeks of hiding, and escape by a stolen dinghy follow.
21460-the-ferryman-of-brill-and-other-st:
The Ferryman of Brill gathers tales by W. H. G. Kingston that first ran in the Quiver magazine. Cassell issued the set in the year of Kingston's death. The first four chapters form the title story, and seven shorter tales follow it.

Brill stands near the broad, slow Meuse, under Spanish rule and the Duke of Alva's harsh hand. A young merchant, Diedrich Meghem, hopes to settle as a rich citizen and perhaps burgomaster. Instead he faces a rival, the Inquisition, and flight to sea. A ferryman proves his true friend in the pinch. Faith and escape drive these tales.
21536-paul-the-minstrel-and-other-storie:
Arthur Christopher Benson gathers romantic tales in Paul the Minstrel and Other Stories, published in 1911. The tales were reprinted from The Hill of Trouble and The Isles of Sunset. Benson was a fellow of Magdalene College, Cambridge, and a famed diarist.

A Burne-Jones line on waking from a fair dream stands at the front. Stories treat the Isles of Sunset, a slype house, a gray cat, and a red camp. Old Mistress Alison and her one honest maid appear in the title tale's world. Each piece works like a picture of a land no one can define, only desire.
21546-nero-the-circus-lion-his-many-adve:
Nero the lion tells his own tale in Richard Barnum's Nero, the Circus Lion, published in 1919. Walter S. Rogers draws Nero leaping through a paper hoop for the front picture. The book belongs to Barnum's Kneetime Animal Stories, with Squinty the pig and Tum Tum the elephant.

Nero starts in a hot jungle land, where low vines hide creeping beasts. The tale follows him from wild cub to circus star, through hunts, capture, and training. Each chapter gives young readers one clear adventure in simple words. Barnum's beasts speak and think like folk, a style that made the series a nursery staple.
21571-the-pacha-of-many-tales:
Captain Marryat lets his invention run riot in The Pacha of Many Tales, published in 1835. The frame tale, modelled on the Arabian Nights, sets a pacha listening to tales. Story within story piles up, in Marryat's sixth book, with glee.

Sailors, slaves, and rogues tell their lives to win the pacha's favour. One grim taste is mocked at the start: a king who decks his steps with fresh heads each day. Marryat said he never knew each morning what he would write. That free hand suits a book built on surprise, where each tale tops the last.
21597-jersey-street-and-jersey-lane-urba:
H. C. Bunner sketches New York's streets in Jersey Street and Jersey Lane, issued in 1896. A. B. Frost and other noted hands drew the pictures. Pieces in the set had run in magazines from 1893 onward.

Jersey and Mulberry opens the set, in the heart of the old city. Later sketches run from Tiemann's to Tubby Hook, and through the Bowery and Bohemia. A story of a path and a lost child add feeling to the fun. Bunner, long the editor of Puck, writes with a kind eye for pushcart folk, pretty girls in windows, and street musicians.
21599-tum-tum-the-jolly-elephant-his-man:
Tum Tum is the jolliest elephant in the circus in Richard Barnum's Tum Tum, the Jolly Elephant, copyrighted in 1915. Before the circus, he was the jolliest elephant in the jungle too. Harriet H. Tooker draws him spraying water on a blazing peanut wagon.

The tale follows Tum Tum from wild days to the big top, trick by trick. Barnum's Kneetime Animal Stories gave each beast a book, from Squinty the pig to Don the dog. Simple words and short chapters suit the youngest readers. Tum Tum's good temper carries him through fires, pranks, and parades with friends.
21612-a-child-of-the-glens-or-elsie-s-fo:
Elsie's fortunes unfold along Ireland's north-east coast in A Child of the Glens, issued in 1875. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published the tale in London and New York. Garron Point and a chain of noble headlands guard the romantic glens.

The coast road from Larne toward Cushendall, forty miles of sea views, frames the tale. Pictures show a clergyman's visit to Tor Bay and a strange waif of the sea. Jim builds castles in the air in another plate. Elsie's trials and blessings play out under those cliffs, in a tale shaped for young, church-going readers.
21630-bibliomania-in-the-middle-ages:
F. Somner Merryweather celebrates book lovers of old in Bibliomania in the Middle Ages, reissued in 1900. Charles Orr, librarian of the Case Library, writes the preface to this New York edition. The subtitle promises sketches of bookworms, collectors, Bible students, scribes, and illuminators.

The tale runs from Anglo-Saxon and Norman times to the coming of print in England. Anecdotes fill out the history of the great monastic libraries of Britain. Orr notes that Merryweather was among the first in English to grant the middle ages their due. Book collecting, he adds, was fashionable in Rome by the first century.
21645-the-romance-of-old-new-england-roo:
Mary C. Crawford tours famous old houses in The Romance of Old New England Rooftrees, copyrighted in 1902. Bishop Berkeley's Whitehall at Newport, built in 1729 and still standing, opens her tales. The book belongs to the Little Pilgrimages series, with many pictures.

Chapters treat the heir of Swift's Vanessa, the maid of Marblehead, and Molly Stark's gentleman son. Doctor Church, the first traitor to the American cause, gets a chapter. So do a woman veteran of the Continental Army and the redeemed captive. Each rooftree shelters a true tale of love, war, or witchcraft days.
21646-how-to-become-rich-a-treatise-on-p:
Professor William Windsor promises wealth through self-knowledge in How to Become Rich, a treatise of 1898. Brain is money and character is capital, his motto runs. Windsor, a phrenologist and anthropologist, also wrote the Science of Creation.

Phrenology, the reading of character from the skull, guides his choice of professions. Later parts treat the choice of a partner in marriage. Windsor owns that fifteen hours of daily practice may have left errors in the text. Modern readers will find the book a rich sample of the self-help and head-reading crazes of the Gilded Age.
21662-hawthorn-and-lavender-with-other-v:
William Ernest Henley gathers songs of love and death in Hawthorn and Lavender, first printed in 1901. He dedicates the verses to his wife of twenty years, who made the man that made the songs. A second edition followed within a month of the first.

A prologue offers the poems to the glory of the green land that bred his women and holds his dead. Shakespeare's line on summer's honey breath stands at the front. Dead things and dying colour the late, autumnal pieces, yet hope and grit run through them. Henley, the model for Long John Silver, writes here in a tenderer key.
21690-flint-his-faults-his-friendships-a:
Maud Wilder Goodwin tells a New England tale in Flint, published at Boston in 1897. A grayish slip pinned to the parlour cushion each Saturday states the board bill. Goodwin calls that brevity characteristic of New England in the lodgers' world she draws.

Chapters move from the day of small things through the old shop and the glorious Fourth. The Mary Ann, Nora Costello, and Flying Point mark places in Flint's fortunes. A soldier, a slum post, and a maiden's vow deepen the tale. Goodwin, who wrote The Head of a Hundred, mixes home life and conscience in a quiet, full novel.
21708-up-in-the-clouds-balloon-voyages:
Balloons carry the action in this book by R. M. Ballantyne, who loved to turn real crafts and trades into stories. The opening chapters trace man's long wish to fly, from early wings to the sad wrecks that ended many bold tries. Men gave up on wings, Ballantyne says, and turned to larger, stranger machines to lift them.

The book then follows balloon voyages and the men who risked them. Ballantyne had studied the subject firsthand, as he did with mines, lifeboats, and lighthouses for his other tales. Readers get both a short history of flight before aeroplanes and a set of sky adventures told in his plain, eager style.
21726-deep-down-a-tale-of-the-cornish-mi:
Cornish mines give Ballantyne the setting for this tale, which begins with a tall young man riding into Penzance with one small bag. Need has driven him to the far end of England to seek his fortune. He walks the last miles to St. Just with a stout stick, set on making up for time lost on the road. The mines wait below, dark and deep.

Ballantyne went down into Cornish mines himself to learn the work before he wrote. The story follows its hero among miners, owners, and the dangers of the deep shafts. Readers get both a gripping tale and a close look at how tin and copper miners lived and labored.
21731-fighting-the-whales:
An old whaler tells his own story in this Ballantyne book, looking back on a life spent fighting whales. He opens with wonder that men can kill a beast sixty feet long, strong as hundreds of horses. One slap of its tail can smash a boat to bits, he says. Yet men hunt it with boats, lines, and nerve.

He recalls starting work as a boy of fifteen in a hard-pressed English seaport town. From there the tale follows the sperm whale hunt across open oceans. Ballantyne mixes fact about whaling with the teller's own hard fights. It is a working sailor's view of one of the most dangerous trades of the age.
21755-personal-reminiscences-in-book-mak:
Looking back over his long writing life, R. M. Ballantyne tells here how his books came to be made. Born in 1825, he went to Canada at sixteen as a Hudson's Bay clerk and came home in 1848. His funny letters home about backwoods life first showed his family that he could write. From them grew The Young Fur Traders, Ungava, and his other northern tales.

Ballantyne also explains his habit of living each trade before he wrote about it: mines, fire brigades, lighthouses, railways, and more. The short stories that follow the memories show the craftsman at work. For readers of his boys' books, this volume is the man himself, plain-spoken about his craft.
21793-obiter-dicta-second-series:
Light essays on books and men of letters fill this second series of Obiter Dicta by Augustine Birrell, issued in a cheap edition in 1896. Birrell opens by joking that critics will say the book has no right to exist. It shows no research, he admits, and he has never been inside the British Museum reading room. It puts forward no theory but one: that literature ought to please.

The essays were written for readers at ease, feet on the fender, glad to be reminded of books once known well. Birrell writes as a friendly talker rather than a scholar. His wit is gentle and his taste is wide. The volume is a small pleasure of Victorian essay writing, meant to be dipped into, not studied.
21794-the-boy-from-the-ranch-or-roy-brad:
Roy Bradner leaves the Triple O ranch for the city in this 1909 boys' novel by Frank V. Webster. A message calls him east, and his father views the trip with suspicion. Roy rides to the train, puzzled by what waits for him. A game on the train and a swindled dude start his education in city ways.

In town he stops a runaway horse, visits the lawyer Caleb Annister, and finds himself in danger and then missing. Chapters carry him through a tenement, a dangerous descent, and a lawyer's advice before the round-up ends the tale. Webster wrote brisk series fiction for boys. Roy's ranch honesty, set against city sharpers, drives every chapter.
21807-the-holy-cross-and-other-tales:
Tales by Eugene Field, the Chicago newspaper poet and humorist, fill this volume first gathered in 1893. Field was loved for his children's verses and his witty columns, and his prose tales show the same mixed moods: serious, gay, and tender. Five tales, beginning with The Platonic Bassoon, were added to the original issue from his later work. Roswell Martin Field, his brother, is honored in the dedication.

The title tale, The Holy Cross, moves its company to gentle pity, as the frontispiece shows. Field writes with a light hand even on sad subjects. This fifth volume of his collected works preserves stories that first lived in newspapers. They show why readers of his day wept and smiled over the same page.
21809-second-book-of-tales:
More tales by Eugene Field make up this second book, gathered in 1896 after the author's death. The editors chose pieces left unpublished in book form, down to The Werewolf. They added eight early sketches from Culture's Garland to show his first manner. The list mixes dialect stories, fairy tales, and tender sketches of mothers and children.

Humin Natur' on the Han'bul 'nd St. Jo tells of a railroad eaten away by war, told in broad dialect. Other tales bring angels, flowers, dream-fairies, and a moon-garden for Sweet-One-Darling. Field could shift from slang to sentiment in a page. The volume, tenth in his collected works, shows the full range of the newspaper storyteller his readers loved.
21824-the-old-stone-house-and-other-stor:
An unfinished stone house in the New York woods opens this set of tales by Anna Katharine Green, first published in 1891. The narrator rides up on a house whose scaffolding was never struck and whose windows mostly lack frames. Moss creeps over the blackened front, and the place feels steeped in tragic mystery. That mystery gives the title story its pull.

The other tales, A Memorable Night, The Black Cross, A Mysterious Case, and Shall He Wed Her?, work in Green's darker vein. Green was a pioneer of the detective novel, and her gift for dread shows here in short form. Gloom, secrets, and slow reveals fill the pages. It is a moody little volume from a mistress of mystery.
21832-the-wonder-island-boys-conquest-of:
War among the island tribes drives this volume of Roger T. Finlay's Wonder Island Boys series, published in 1914. Sutoto startles the camp, and the Tuolos, Kurabus, and Illyas draw together in confederation. A council of chiefs hears the case for unity against their common foes. Oma, Uraso, and Muro give their views before the allied tribes meet in the field.

The series follows two boys and an aged professor cast away with nothing, building every tool of civilized life step by step. Finlay folds science and craft into the fighting and scouting. Each book stands alone, and this one brings the tribal wars to their climax. Boys of the day got battle, invention, and two thousand facts in one cloth binding.
21863-derrick-sterling-a-story-of-the-mi:
Coal country dangers drive this boys' novel by Kirk Munroe, Derrick Sterling: A Story of the Mines, published by Harpers in 1888. The tale opens with cries of fire in the burning breaker, where boys work above the pits. White-faced miners of the night shift crowd the slope mouth as the chapters roll on. Derrick moves through a fearful ride, a lost wander in the mine, and a plunge down an air shaft.

A fatal explosion of fire-damp, a flooded mine, and a rescue fill the later chapters. Harry the bumping-mule and Socrates the wise mine rat give relief. Munroe knew hard trades and wrote them true. The book honors the boys who worked underground, and ends with Derrick promoted and restored to daylight.
21869-immortal-memories:
Toastmaster's speeches on great writers fill Clement Shorter's Immortal Memories, talks given to literary societies and gathered in 1907. Shorter admits in his preface that the addresses pleased him to write and seemed to interest their audiences. He aims them, he says, not at fellow journalists but at Hazlitt's sensible people: men of business and of the world.

One toast recalls a dear friend who proposed it the year before and has since died. Lord Acton's famous list of the hundred best books turns up in the talk. Shorter was a tireless champion of the Brontës and of popular literature. These speeches show him at the dinner table: warm, bookish, and quotable, keeping dead authors in living company.
21927-short-cruises:
Wapping sailors and their wives scheme and blunder through W. W. Jacobs's Short Cruises, a set of comic tales published in 1906. The first story, The Changeling, opens with George Henshaw wiping his boots in a too-still house, his wife's blazing stare waiting in the kitchen. Other tales bring mixed relations, a love-knot, a dreamer, and angels' visits. Jacobs's illustrations captions alone raise a smile: soft brown eyes, sarcasm, and a mate who smiled too.

Jacobs made the Thames waterfront his comic kingdom, and these short pieces show his hand at its surest. The humor is dry, the dialogue salted with dialect, and the plots turn on small vanities. Readers who know his longer novels will find the same world in miniature, perfectly timed.
21958-frank-merriwell-s-races:
Frank Merriwell goes to the races in this 1903 number of Burt L. Standish's famous dime-novel series. Diamond walks round Frank's bay gelding on the stable floor and calls him a swift one: rangey, clean-limbed, with a courageous eye. Horse talk leads to plots, eavesdroppers, and a strong accusation against the cleanest hero in American cheap fiction.

The chapters pile on a wrestling match, a boat race, a spurned bribe, and a fight on a special train. Yale spirit and pure grit carry Frank through every trap. Standish, whose real name was Gilbert Patten, built Merriwell into a national model of the all-round college man. This volume mixes the turf with the campus, and lets Frank win both ways, honestly.
21965-preventable-diseases:
Most sickness can be stopped before it starts, argues Dr. Woods Hutchinson in Preventable Diseases, published in 1909. Hutchinson, a clinical professor of medicine in New York, calls the body a republic with its own defenses. He grants that the human machine is imperfect, beaten at points by animals and machines alike. Yet heredity, air, and habits lie in our own hands, he insists.

Chapters take up colds and how we catch them, adenoids and mouth-breathing, pneumonia, and typhoid's natural history. Tuberculosis gets two chapters as a scotched snake, not a dead one. The writing is brisk, funny, and aimed at lay readers. The book helped carry the new gospel of prevention into ordinary homes.
21979-for-name-and-fame-or-through-afgha:
A lost child grows into a soldier of the Afghan war in G. A. Henty's For Name and Fame, or Through Afghan Passes. Sam Dickson finds little Willie Gale, and the foundling's road runs from a fishing smack through shipwreck and a fight with prahus to India. Henty's preface promises that following Will through the last Afghan war will teach a country of supreme importance to the British Empire. Lord Roberts's operations frame the hero's service.

The Peiwar Kotal, the Khyber advance, the massacre at Kabul, Maiwand, and Kandahar fill the war chapters. Will saves Colonel Ripon and is carried by a bayonet in the pictures. Henty mixes a boy's rise with a campaign history. It is his classic recipe: geography and glory, taught through one lad's luck.
22014-the-peter-patter-book-of-nursery-r:
Leroy F. Jackson wrote the rhymes in The Peter Patter Book of Nursery Rhymes, first issued in 1918. Blanche Fisher Wright drew the pictures. Peter Patter himself lives on a mountain near the sun, in a home among the alders. Squirrels, crickets, bats, and his Uncle Owl bring him every rhyme he knows.

The verses that follow are new nursery rhymes rather than the old Mother Goose stock. Goats, kings, platters of brisket and batter, and small boys fill the pages. Each rhyme is short, musical, and made to be read aloud. The book went on being reprinted for decades, with its copyright renewed in 1946.
22085-sir-jagadis-chunder-bose-his-life-:
Jagadis Chunder Bose was born in Bengal in 1858, in a village in the Dacca district. He grew up at Faridpur, where his father served as a local officer. The boy who watched plants and weather there became one of India's first modern scientists. Bose won world fame for work on wireless waves and on the responses of plants to touch, light, and wounds.

Sir Jagadis Chunder Bose: His Life and Speeches combines a biography with his own addresses. The life draws on his boyhood, schooling, and struggles for a laboratory in Calcutta. The speeches let Bose argue his case himself. The volume is a period tribute to a scientist who proved an Indian could lead world research.
22087-hazel-squirrel-and-other-stories:
Howard B. Famous wrote Hazel Squirrel and Other Stories for young children who like their heroes small and furry. Hazel is a young squirrel with a bad habit of hurrying. One morning he ties his tie sideways and brushes his tail the wrong way. He even forgets the breakfast his mother left out for him.

The other stories follow woodland animals through small scrapes and small lessons. Each tale is short enough for a single reading at bedtime. Manners, kindness, and care for one's mother come wrapped in fur and whiskers. Such animal storybooks were a staple of American childhood in the early 1900s, and Hazel is a typical busy hero.
22114-a-plain-cookery-book-for-the-worki:
Charles Elmé Francatelli, once cook to Queen Victoria, wrote A Plain Cookery Book for the Working Classes in 1852. Francatelli aimed his skill at the poorest kitchens in England. Every recipe counts pennies and wastes nothing. Broths, puddings, cheap cuts, and vegetables fill the little book.

He gives exact measures and plain steps a beginner can follow. Even a breakfast-cup custard is broken down spoonful by spoonful. The book was sold cheaply and pushed by reformers who hoped good cooking would fight hunger and drink. It remains a landmark of social cookery, and a sharp record of what the Victorian poor could afford to eat.
22145-a-book-of-burlesques:
H. L. Mencken, the Baltimore critic, gathered A Book of Burlesques in 1916. These short pieces mock the solemn forms of his day: plays, sermons, novels, and official prose. One sketch opens with stage directions for a suffocating room, flowers everywhere, as if it rained outside, which it isn't. The joke lands before a word of dialogue is spoken.

Mencken's targets include puritans, professors, uplifters, and literary poseurs. His sentences snap; his slang was new and shocking in 1916. The burlesques are juvenilia by his later standard, but the voice is already his. Readers meeting Mencken here meet the sage of Baltimore warming up his famous act.
22168-the-golden-spears-and-other-fairy-:
Edmund Leamy, an Irish writer of fairy tales, published The Golden Spears and Other Fairy Tales in 1911. Corinne Turner drew the pictures. The title tale takes its name from an Irish mountain. The peak is bare and grey at its top. Yet it catches the sinking sun until it gleams like a spear of gold. So the children call it the Golden Spear.

Leamy retells Irish legends and wonder tales in gentle, literary English. Kings, heroes, and fairy folk move through his pages. He wrote to keep Ireland's old stories alive for children losing them. The book belongs to the Celtic revival's nursery shelf, where myth was handed down as national treasure.
22194-spring-street-a-story-of-los-angel:
Spring Street calls itself a story of Los Angeles, and it belongs to the city's early fiction. Children shout at a wild game a few doors down the street. Suddenly they stop, warned to be quiet: a neighbour has died, and the street must hush. The narrator remembers his own childhood shock at a death nearby, struck dumb for days.

From such street scenes the novel builds its Los Angeles. Spring Street was then the city's busy financial and shopping spine. Booth and local colour fill the pages in period style. The book survives as a curiosity of regional writing, when Los Angeles was still inventing itself in fiction as fast as in fact.
22195-little-tora-the-swedish-schoolmist:
Little Tora, the Swedish Schoolmistress, and Other Stories gathers tales of Sweden for English readers. The title story concerns Tora, a young schoolmistress in a Swedish village. One scene shows a family dinner laid in state: polished silver, shining glass, porcelain, flowers, and fruit cover the table. The plenty on the table seems, at first, to be all the dinner there is.

Mrs. Woods Baker, who wrote several books of Swedish life, gathered these tales from her years in Sweden. Village customs, schools, and family pride shape the plots. Such translated collections introduced English children to Scandinavian childhood. This one keeps the quiet, moral tone of the Swedish originals.
22198-two-sides-of-the-face-midwinter-ta:
Arthur Quiller-Couch, who signed himself "Q," published Two Sides of the Face as a set of midwinter tales. Quiller-Couch was a Cornish writer, anthologist, and champion of clear English. The title story opens behind a house where fields have cut back a plantation of noble ash trees. The modern farm buildings, shabby as they are, look friendlier than the old mansion brooding above them.

That contrast of faces, cheerful front and lost dignity, runs through the tales. Ghosts, doubles, and old houses suit the midwinter season of the subtitle. Quiller-Couch writes with a storyteller's ease and a scholar's vocabulary. The collection shows his fiction at its most characteristic: Cornish air, quiet uncanniness.
22217-my-reminiscences:
Rabindranath Tagore, the Bengali poet who won the Nobel Prize in 1913, wrote My Reminiscences about his own formation.
